**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Working Group
**Re:** Buy more GPUs, or use the ones we have better?
**Date:** [Internal circulation only]

We've reached the point in our quarterly planning where the hardware question resurfaces, and I want to lay out my thinking before we meet on Thursday. The short version: I believe we should spend the next quarter aggressively improving utilisation of the hardware we already own, and only revisit purchasing if that effort demonstrably fails. The longer version follows.

The instinct to buy is understandable. Our queue times during the last two sprint cycles were genuinely painful, and several experiments were shelved simply because nobody wanted to wait forty minutes for a fine-tuning run to return. But when I dug into the actual telemetry, the picture was less "we don't have enough hardware" and more "we are using what we have remarkably badly." Across the fleet, our average GPU utilisation sits somewhere in the low thirties, and a meaningful fraction of that is memory-bound inference jobs that could run on smaller cards or, in some cases, on CPU. Meanwhile, our most expensive accelerators sit idle overnight and most weekends because we never built a scheduler that could fill those windows with batch work.

That gap between peak demand and average utilisation is exactly where the money is. A new node would cost us not just the capital price, which is substantial at current market rates, but the operational overhead of power, cooling, rack space, and the maintenance contract we'd inevitably need. It would also take six to eight weeks to arrive, during which our utilisation problem would remain untouched. By contrast, the work to fix scheduling, right-size job placement, and introduce basic queueing with priorities is almost entirely engineering time we already control. The opportunity cost cuts both ways, of course: every week an engineer spends on the scheduler is a week not spent on product work. But that trade is bounded and cheap compared to a hardware commitment that will follow us for three to five years.

Latency deserves its own mention, because it's the argument I find hardest to dismiss. Interactive work, notebook sessions, and the demo pipeline genuinely suffer when the fleet is saturated, and no amount of clever scheduling fully removes the queuing delay a researcher feels at two in the afternoon when everyone else is also pushing jobs. If our goal were to make the interactive experience uniformly excellent at peak hours, more hardware would be the honest answer. But I don't think that's our goal right now. Most of our latency complaints trace to a handful of recurring batch jobs that were scheduled by habit rather than design, and simply moving those to off-peak windows would relieve the majority of the contention we see. We should test that hypothesis before buying our way out of it.

Reliability is the quieter argument, and I want to give it weight. Our current fleet has a single-node failure mode that has bitten us twice: when one machine goes down, certain workloads have no fallback, and we lose a day. Buying more hardware would incidentally improve redundancy, but it would do so expensively and indirectly. We could get most of the same resilience by making our jobs checkpointable and portable across the machines we already have, which is work we should want to do regardless of what we own. Reliability bought through architecture tends to age better than reliability bought through redundancy alone.

There's also the question of reversibility, and here I think the asymmetry strongly favours the software path. Scheduler improvements, checkpointing, and job right-sizing are all reversible decisions. If they don't pay off, we've lost some engineering weeks and gained a better understanding of our workload profile. A hardware purchase is largely irreversible. Accelerator generations turn over quickly, resale values are poor, and the depreciation clock starts the moment the crate is opened. If our workload mix shifts, as it has twice in the past year, a fleet sized for yesterday's jobs becomes a liability rather than an asset. Buying hardware now, before we understand our true demand curve, risks locking us into capacity shaped by a snapshot of a moving target.

I want to be honest about the uncertainty here. My utilisation numbers come from a monitoring stack we all agree is imperfect, and it's possible that beneath the averages there's a hard ceiling of genuinely concurrent demand that our current fleet cannot meet no matter how well we schedule. If, after a quarter of focused effort, peak-hour contention remains severe and the interactive experience is still poor, then the case for purchasing becomes strong, and we'll be making that decision with far better data than we have today. That's the real value of waiting: not avoidance of the decision, but deferral of it until the evidence is worth acting on.

My recommendation, then: commit the next quarter to utilisation work, set an explicit threshold for what constitutes failure, and schedule the hardware decision for the start of the following quarter with real numbers in hand. If we're going to spend that money, let's spend it knowing exactly what we're buying and why.

Happy to discuss Thursday.

Here is the reasoning, along with the caveats we think matter.

The starting point is that our current fleet is measurably underused. Telemetry from the past eight weeks shows average GPU utilisation across our four A100 nodes sitting around 38 percent, with a diurnal pattern that leaves the overnight window almost entirely idle. Peak demand, concentrated in the late afternoon when the research team runs evaluation sweeps, pushes two of the four nodes above 90 percent while the others remain half-empty. This is not a capacity problem in the aggregate; it is a scheduling and fragmentation problem. Jobs are pinned to specific nodes by habit and by legacy configuration rather than by a scheduler that sees the whole fleet. A modest investment in a proper queueing layer, containerised job packaging, and checkpoint-resume support would let us pack work dynamically and absorb the overnight idle capacity into batch workloads like fine-tuning runs and dataset preprocessing that don't need interactive latency.

The economics reinforce this. A new node costs roughly the capital price of the hardware plus power, cooling, and — the number people forget — the ongoing engineering time to integrate, monitor, and maintain it. Our estimate is that better scheduling could raise effective utilisation from 38 to around 65 percent, which is equivalent to adding roughly 1.7 nodes of throughput for a fraction of the cost of buying even one. The opportunity cost matters too: the engineering time a purchase would consume in procurement, racking, and integration is time we would otherwise spend on the scheduling work itself, and the scheduling work benefits every workload we run, not just the marginal one that triggered the discussion.

Latency considerations cut both ways, and we want to be honest about that. Interactive workloads — the notebook-style experimentation the research team depends on — genuinely suffer when queues form. If utilisation improvements were implemented naively, a researcher could find themselves waiting behind a six-hour batch job. The mitigation is well understood: priority classes, preemption with checkpointing, and reserving headroom on at least one node for interactive use. Done properly, latency for interactive work should actually improve, because today's contention comes from uncoordinated manual job placement rather than from any principled allocation. But this is the part of the plan most likely to go wrong in practice, and it needs careful rollout with the research team in the loop.

Reliability is a quieter argument for the utilisation path. Adding hardware adds failure modes: another node to patch, another set of drivers and firmware to keep consistent, another component in our failure domain. Consolidating work onto a well-scheduled fleet we already understand, with proven monitoring and known failure behaviour, is lower-risk operationally than expanding the estate. It also forces a useful discipline — if a job can't be checkpointed and rescheduled, that fragility is worth surfacing now rather than after we've doubled the fleet.

The strongest argument for buying now is reversibility in the other direction: hardware lead times are long, and if demand genuinely grows, ordering late means waiting. We take this seriously. Our answer is that the decision is not irreversible in the way it first appears. A quarter of utilisation work gives us real data on whether demand is saturating true capacity or merely fragmenting it, and cloud burst capacity — spot instances from a mainstream provider — covers a genuine short-term shortfall at acceptable cost for the batch workloads most likely to overflow. That makes the buy decision reversible and better-informed later, whereas buying now locks in capital and operating commitments on the basis of a utilisation number we already know is distorted.

We acknowledge the uncertainty honestly. Our utilisation figures come from node-level telemetry, which can undercount or overcount depending on how memory residency is measured, and our 65 percent target is an estimate, not a guarantee. If the scheduling work stalls, or if the research roadmap adds a training programme that needs dedicated sustained capacity, the purchase case strengthens considerably, and we should revisit at that point rather than defending this recommendation out of inertia.
